title: A full round
hook: Rama gives Hanuman 108; the mala's full round
carry: the mala: one full round of 108

segments.voice: Yesterday, ajapa, and Valmiki's name that turned itself around. Your line was japa goes inward until japa goes inward until it says itself. Today, the end of mantra week, and your first full round.
screen: `JAPA GOES INWARD UNTIL JAPA GOES INWARD UNTIL IT SAYS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Pick up a japa mala, a string of prayer beads, and count. Very often: one hundred and eight. Plus one more, bigger, set apart, often with a tassel. Gods have lists of 108 names, recited as one long litany of praise. Some sacred places are counted in sets of 108. The number keeps turning up. Ask people why, and you'll get plenty of confident answers, and they won't match.
screen: `108 BEADS, PLUS ONE.` → `108 NAMES, 108 PLACES.` → `MANY ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Nobody knows for certain why 108; people give many answers, and they don't match. But one text shows how it came to mean complete. It's a conversation in Ayodhya, after the war. Hanuman, who leapt the ocean and carried the mountain, sits at Rama's feet and asks what every seeker asks: how does anyone get free? Rama answers in a short text called the Muktika Upanishad. One Upanishad is enough, he says, if you truly take it in. If not, ten. If not, thirty-two. And if not, here are a hundred and eight, the full set: take these in, and you'll be free. So 108 became one of the tradition's ways of saying the whole. There are lists of 108 names for Vishnu, for Shiva, for the Goddess, for Ganesha. And there's the japa mala: 108 beads, plus one big bead, the meru, named for the mountain at the center of the world, and also called the guru bead. Here's how a round works. Hold the mala in your right hand, over the middle finger, and pull each bead toward you with your thumb, one bead per mantra. Many teachers say to keep the index finger off the beads. When you come back to the meru, you don't cross it; many explain that you don't step over the guru. For another round, turn the mala around and go back the way you came. And that's the week: Ganesha's seed, the name sung together, the Gayatri at dawn, the name going inward. Now one full round of 108: a whole offering, start to finish.
screen: `HANUMAN ASKS: HOW DOES ANYONE GET FREE?` · `ONE. TEN. THIRTY-TWO. 108.` · `THE MERU: THE GURU BEAD.` · `DON'T CROSS IT. TURN BACK.` · then, large: `THE MALA: ONE FULL ROUND OF 108.`

segments.voice: Pick your mantra, the one that fits, or Om, or Om Namah Shivaya, and begin beside the big bead, or on your finger joints, twelve per hand counted with the thumb, nine times through. One bead, one mantra, softly or silently; the bell will ring before you finish, and that's fine, so keep going until you reach the meru. Then don't start another; sit for three breaths.
Meru, the big bead you stop at, not cross: the guru bead ending the mala's 108, one full round, complete.
Your line: the mala, one full round of 108. The whole set, as Rama gave it, and then you rest. Mantra week, done.

howItsDone: Hindus doing japa commonly use a mala of 108 beads plus a larger meru bead, moving one bead per mantra with the thumb and middle finger, and turning back at the meru rather than crossing it; one full round is 108 repetitions.

Hanuman.meaning: Rama's devoted helper, who leapt the ocean

Muktika Upanishad.meaning: a late Upanishad in which Rama lists 108 Upanishads

notes: 'The distance from the earth to the sun is about 108 times the sun's width' — approximately true (about 107.5 solar diameters). Framed as 'some point out'. Keeper may prefer to drop it.
Mala technique (draped over the middle finger, thumb pulls, index finger kept away, not crossing the meru) varies by lineage. Confirm.

Finger-joint counting: 12 joints per hand (excluding thumbs) — a common method is counting 12 then tracking with the other hand; '12 per hand, nine times through' is the writer's simplification. Confirm.
Outline practice '108' exceeds the 2-minute sit; the practice invites continuing past the bell.
